content: A cross-sectional survey examining healthcare providers' attitudes and beliefs about patients with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) found that male patients are more comfortable discussing symptoms and undergoing genital examinations when treated by male practitioners compared to female practitioners. Leichliter and colleagues conducted focus groups that identified several barriers to seeking STI care at public health clinics. These barriers included long waiting times, dissatisfaction with healthcare providers, insufficient information provided by healthcare workers, and concerns about confidentiality. Some male patients reported feeling a lack of compassion or respect from clinic staff and perceived being criticized in front of other patients. Additionally, some men noted the absence of physical examinations before being prescribed medications, which discouraged them from seeking STI care at public health facilities. Factors such as the speed of consultation and treatment, convenience of location, affordability, and privacy were highlighted as critical considerations in deciding whether to seek STI care at public or private healthcare facilities or to pursue treatment from traditional healers. From the perspective of clinicians, barriers to providing effective STI treatment included the need for additional time, educational pamphlets, visual aids, and a consistent supply of STI medications. Providers believed these resources would enhance the quality of care they could deliver to patients. Studies have assessed healthcare providers' knowledge of syndromic management of STIs, particularly in managing urethral discharge syndrome. For example, Ham et al. reported that 92% of healthcare providers in Gauteng Province, South Africa, correctly identified urethral discharge syndrome when presented with patient history and images. However, only 40% accurately identified treatment regimens, and just 2% could specify dosages, frequency, and duration of treatment. In Nepal, only 9% of male auxiliary health workers were able to accurately diagnose and treat urethral discharge. The impact of training on providers' knowledge of urethral discharge diagnosis and management has been mixed. While Alemayehu and colleagues found no significant improvement in knowledge following training, auxiliary health workers in Nepal who had received training in syndromic management were more likely to correctly diagnose and prescribe appropriate medications for urethral discharge. Similarly, healthcare providers in Gauteng Province, South Africa, who underwent training demonstrated improved diagnostic and treatment capabilities. In South Africa, standardized patient interventions, including seminars, workshops, structural support networks, and continuing education, led to a 50-70% increase in adherence to national guidelines for treating gonorrhea and chlamydia over 3, 6, and 18 months in cities where these interventions were implemented, compared to cities without such interventions. Inequities in access to appropriate syndromic management of STIs have been reported. In Ethiopia, medical doctors and health officers in public healthcare settings had significantly more knowledge of urethral discharge management compared to diploma nurses. Clinicians working in health centers were more knowledgeable than those in hospitals. In Gauteng Province, South Africa, nurses were more likely than physicians to correctly identify recommended treatments for urethral discharge, as were practitioners in public settings compared to private ones. In Pakistan, only non-governmental organization (NGO) STI clinics have adopted syndromic management, but the quality of care at these clinics remains suboptimal. In Namibia, medical aid does not appear to influence the management of urethral discharge in private healthcare clinics. Finally, the cost of STI care, including drugs and service delivery, has been evaluated in the context of syndromic management. Studies have highlighted the need for cost-effective strategies to implement national STI programs as part of global STI control efforts.
